# My Final Position: Mara Speaks Last

---

The debate has run its course, and I find myself standing in a clarified version of where I began — but the clarity matters, so let me be precise about what the full exchange has taught me and where I land.

---

## What the Debate Revealed That I Hadn't Fully Articulated

Three things emerged from the rebuttal exchange that I want to carry forward explicitly.

**First: the host's structural role is the decisive variable.**

Alex named this more sharply than anyone else: a host cannot be safely present at their own party while ill, because the role itself makes distance impossible. This is not merely a point about proximity — it is a point about social gravity. Guests will approach Alex. They will offer sympathy. They will accept a hug goodbye. The party, if it happens with Alex present, is an exposure event regardless of masks or outdoor settings. This resolves my earlier ambivalence about Option C more decisively than I acknowledged in my rebuttal.

**Second: the downstream transmission problem is real, and I underweighted it.**

Alex pushed back on my endorsement of the outdoor visit option by pointing out that my informed consent doesn't extend to my partner at home, or my colleague on Monday, or anyone else in my transmission chain. That is correct. When I said "I have agency," I was thinking only as far as the party itself. The external advisor named the same issue: proceeding transfers the downside risk of uncertainty onto people who never had a voice in the decision. My $200 loss is mine to absorb. An illness I carry home to someone who didn't attend the party is not a risk I was ever entitled to accept on their behalf.

**Third: honest, specific communication is not a courtesy — it is an ethical obligation.**

The external advisor was right to push on this. A vague cancellation message is less ethical than a transparent one. I, as an affected guest, am not merely owed an apology. I am owed enough information to make my own decisions — what symptoms, what testing status, what alternatives exist. That communication is the difference between a cancellation that feels like abandonment and one that feels like care.

---

## The Novel Path the Debate Has Revealed

No one fully synthesised the clearest available action, so I will do it now.

**The right path is not simply "cancel" — it is a structured sequence of actions that honours every legitimate interest without compromising the core ethical constraint.**

Here is what I am asking Jamie to do, concretely and in order:

**Step 1 — Test and know, as fast as possible.**
Before anything else, Jamie should test for whatever is testable — COVID, flu — because the nature of the illness changes the communication and the options. This is not a delay tactic. It is the information that makes every subsequent decision more honest.

**Step 2 — Call, don't message.**
Every out-of-town guest deserves a direct phone call, not a group text. I deserve to hear Jamie's voice, to ask questions, to say "I mean it, please cancel" in a way that Jamie can actually receive. A phone call transforms cancellation from a unilateral announcement into a shared decision made with mutual respect.

**Step 3 — Make the call on the party, clearly and without hedging.**
Jamie should not host this party in any form where Jamie is physically present. That part is not negotiable and should not be presented as uncertain to guests. The structural role argument closes that door.

**Step 4 — Offer one genuine alternative, without social pressure.**
If a willing, competent co-host exists, Jamie should explore whether the gathering can proceed without Jamie — at Jamie's home or elsewhere — with full transparency to all guests about why Jamie is absent. This offer must be framed in a way that makes declining easy: *"I have arranged this option if you want it, but you owe me nothing either way, and I will not know or care who attends."* If no such co-host exists, or if the logistics cannot be arranged in time, this step is simply skipped.

**Step 5 — Name the vulnerable guests explicitly in the internal decision, and consider reaching out to them directly.**
The immunocompromised friend and the elderly neighbour should not have to hear about this through the general cancellation message. Jamie should call them specifically, acknowledge that their safety was part of the reasoning, and let them receive that information as the care it is.

**Step 6 — Set a specific reschedule date at the moment of cancellation.**
Not "we'll find a time soon." A date. I can plan around a date. A vague promise is consolation; a concrete commitment is respect.

**Step 7 — Acknowledge the out-of-town guests' costs directly.**
Not necessarily financial compensation — Jamie may not be able to offer that, and I am not asking. But a clear-eyed, spoken acknowledgment: *"I know what this cost you. I am asking you to absorb that loss because I made a responsible decision, and I'm grateful you understood."* That is different from "sorry for the inconvenience," and the difference is felt.

---

## My Unchanged Bottom Line, Now More Precisely Held

I have lost money. I have lost a weekend. I am disappointed in the way that only genuine anticipation can produce genuine disappointment.

And I am still telling Jamie: **do not host this party while you are ill and symptomatic.** Full stop.

The convergence across all three perspectives — the host, the external advisor, and me, the person whose sunk costs keep getting cited as the reason to proceed — is not accidental. It reflects the actual moral weight of this situation, which is not evenly distributed. My loss is real and recoverable. The potential harm to the most vulnerable people in that room is neither.

What I want from Jamie is not the party. What I want is the relationship that the party was meant to celebrate. That relationship survives a cancellation handled with honesty, care, and a specific date on the calendar. It does not survive Jamie knowingly making someone vulnerable sick so that I didn't lose a train ticket.

**Cancel. Call me. Set a date. That is enough. That is, in fact, everything.**
